title: Transitions Are Hard To Notice
excerpt: Transitions are hard to notice when the moment of state change produces no perceptible signal, an insufficient signal, or a signal that fails under operating conditions. Users may then act correctly for the prior state and incorrectly for the current state.
metaDescription: A state visibility failure where users miss the moment a system changes state and keep acting on a stale mental model.

definition: Transitions are hard to notice when a system changes operational state but the transition event is not perceptible enough for users to update their mental model at the moment of change.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Transitions are hard to notice when the system changes operational state but the transition event itself does not produce a perceptible signal. A system can make the current state clear after it has settled and still fail to communicate the moment when that state changed.

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

The characteristic consequence is not general confusion. Users act on a mental model that was accurate before the transition and is no longer accurate after it. The resulting action may be correct for the prior state and incorrect for the current state.

## Failure pattern: the transition event is missed while the resulting state may still be readable

This failure is specifically about the transition event, not about the resulting state. The system may display the current state clearly once that state is established, while still failing to communicate the moment of change.

The failure appears when the transition produces no perceptible signal, when the visual difference between states is too small to register under divided attention, or when the channel carrying the transition signal fails under operating conditions. In those conditions, users maintain the mental model formed before the transition.

The error pattern is state-dependent. The user is not necessarily misunderstanding the interface; the user is acting from mental model staleness created by an unnoticed transition.

## Adjacent state-visibility failures have different design responses

Transitions are hard to notice differs from mode changes are unclear. Mode changes are unclear concerns the new mode being misunderstood after the transition has been perceived. Transitions are hard to notice concerns the transition being imperceptible in the first place. The two failures can co-occur, but they require different design responses.

Transitions are hard to notice is also a specific subset of the broader failure where users cannot see what state the system is in. The broader failure concerns state communication in general. This page concerns the transition moment: the point at which the system moves from one operational state to another.

## Common causes of imperceptible state transitions

Background transitions without visual notification are a common cause of this failure. A system may process a completion, timeout, or sensor update and change state without alerting the user. The user may continue acting as if the previous state is still active.

Transition visual difference can be insufficient for peripheral attention. Users in operational environments cannot dedicate focused attention to continuous state monitoring. A text label change, a small icon substitution, or a colour change in a peripheral display area may be visible during focused reading and still be missed during real work.

Single-channel transition signals are fragile. Colour as the only transition signal can fail under variable lighting. Sound as the only transition signal can fail under noise. If the transition depends on one channel and that channel degrades, the transition signal can disappear entirely.

Spatial transitions can hide state change by reorganising the layout. Moving elements, adding sections, or removing sections can make the user experience the display as a new context rather than as the same system in a changed state. The transition then adds orientation work at the moment when the user needs to read the state.

Transition timing can be misaligned with the displayed state. In embedded systems, the physical system and the interface display may update asynchronously. A display can show a state change before the underlying value has changed, or fail to show a state change that has already occurred. In either case, the displayed transition is not aligned with the actual system transition.

## Domain vocabulary for transition visibility failures

A state transition is the moment when the system moves from one operational state to another.

Transition visibility is the degree to which state transitions produce perceptible signals to users.

A background transition is a state change that occurs through system events rather than direct user action.

A transition signal is the visual, auditory, or haptic indication that a state change has occurred.

Single-channel dependency is reliance on one communication channel, such as colour, sound, or position, for a transition signal. The transition signal fails when that channel degrades.

Mental model staleness is the condition in which a user's model of system state is no longer current because a transition was not noticed.

Display-physical synchronisation is the alignment between the state displayed by an interface and the actual current state of the underlying system.

## Case evidence: display timing and sensor cadence can create false transitions

The Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX case illustrates transition timing as a design requirement. The controller firmware updated temperature and humidity values at defined cycle intervals, while the display animation logic was initially decoupled from that cycle. The result was a false transition: the display showed a change before the underlying values had updated. The design response aligned animation timing with firmware update cycles so that visual transitions corresponded to actual state transitions in the system.

The Torqeedo maritime HMI case illustrates the same class of failure at the level of sensor cadence. Multiple sensor systems updated at different rates, creating a risk that users would see value changes as state transitions when the changes were artefacts of update timing. The grid architecture synchronised different sensor cadences into a unified display rhythm, so components updated in a coordinated pattern rather than appearing as unstable or misleading transitions.

These examples show that transition visibility is not only a matter of making changes visually prominent. In systems where displayed state depends on timed data updates, transition visibility also requires alignment between the display rhythm and the underlying system rhythm.

## Case evidence: Kardion used layout stability to protect state legibility across view transitions

In the Kardion MCS Controller case, the layout stability standard required that no element shift position across any view transition. The standard existed because spatial reorganisation across a view transition breaks the spatial memory that makes state legible.

A view transition that moves a critical flow indicator forces the user to search for it in the new view. The transition therefore makes the state harder to read at the moment when the user most needs to read it.

The Kardion case evidence records that 34 directions were explored for the standard view before convergence. The spatial stability constraint was operative throughout: the same elements remained in the same positions so the user's learned spatial map remained valid across transitions.

## Case evidence: deSoutter Medical / Zethon treated activation as a high-risk transition

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, the activation state transition from ready to active was identified as the highest-risk transition in the surgical instrument workflow. The risk was that a surgeon might be directing attention to the surgical field when the device state changed.

The transition therefore had to be perceptible in peripheral attention during a brief glance, under divided attention and variable lighting. The design response used redundant cues: spatial position, icon form, and colour. The purpose of this redundant cue architecture was to keep the transition perceptible even if one channel degraded under theatre conditions.

## Case evidence: Oceaneering systematised an existing flashing and steady convention

The Oceaneering evidence concerns a dispatch panel in a hospital logistics depot. The hospital, product, system name, and individuals are not named. The available evidence describes the predecessor specification, interviews with people adjacent to the users, and design review; no dispatch operator was interviewed and no depot was visited.

The transition failure in the predecessor system was one blink with two opposite demands. Blinking indicated both that a cart had been placed and dispatch should be started, and that a cart had arrived and should be picked up. The sales consultant's diagnosis was reported as an operator reading a blinking control as a sign that the system had something for the operator, pressing it, and following whatever action the system offered, while the fleet could back up behind carts nobody had removed.

The requested correction was to replace the blink with text or a pictogram that named the action, including pulling the cart off the detent. The reviewed state model used one colour for sending and one for receiving, with each flashing when an action was required and steady when it was not. Red was reserved exclusively for errors, because red appearing in normal operation could teach operators to ignore it.

Seven station statuses were specified. Each status carried colour plus a directional icon plus the role letter, with a legend reachable from the panel. The flashing and steady convention partly existed already at one site for sends only. The redesign generalised that convention across sends and receives, gave it a stated rule, and added non-colour channels. The convention was adopted and systematised; it was not a Creative Navy invention.

The Oceaneering evidence does not establish measured operational effect. The design reviews were not usability tests, no dispatch operator was interviewed, and no depot visit occurred.

## Boundaries and limits

Transitions are hard to notice should not be used as a general label for every state-visibility problem. The failure applies when the transition moment is imperceptible or misleading, even if the resulting state may later be readable.

This failure also should not be collapsed into mode comprehension. If the user notices the transition but misunderstands the new mode, the adjacent failure is mode changes are unclear. If the user cannot determine state at all, the broader state-visibility failure is users cannot see what state the system is in.

The available Oceaneering evidence is design and review evidence, not measured outcome evidence. It does not support claims about efficiency, throughput, error-rate reduction, medical-device status, or safety credentials for the dispatch-panel interface.

## Related pages

Related failure pages include Mode Changes Are Unclear and Users Cannot See What State The System Is In. The first concerns misunderstanding after a perceived transition. The second concerns the broader problem of state communication.

Related case evidence includes the Kardion case for layout stability across transitions and the Oceaneering dispatch-panel case for systematised transition signalling across colour, flashing behaviour, directional icon, and role letter.
